newsitem.title: SYRIA: Chirac tones down call for EU Mideast role.
newsitem.headline: Chirac tones down call for EU Mideast role.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac toned down his call for the European Union to co-sponsor the Middle East peace process on Sunday in the light of Israeli hostility but said Europe had every reason to be involved.
At a joint news conference with Syrian President Hafez al-Assad, Chirac said: "I did not come here to teach people lessons...Naturally we are not trying to force our way in.
"I am simply saying that we are available and that we have valid reasons to be involved, and that a certain balance of things may justify the presence of Europe and of France."

The French leader struck a more cautious note after Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy bluntly said there was no need for another mediator in Arab-Israeli negotiations and such ambitions could be harmful.

Chirac, who flies on to Israel on Monday for what seems certain to be the most difficult stage of his seven-day tour of the region, also praised the United States' mediation role in the past and at present.

He had omitted any mention of Washington, the dominant power broker in the region, from a dinner speech on Saturday in which he said the time had come for Europe to co-sponsor the stalled peace process, contributing proposals and not just money.

Calling Chirac "my great friend, my very dear friend...and a friend of Syria", Assad declared the French leader's visit a success and thanked him for accomplishing "a task of very great importance for the peace process in the region".
Syria and France signed two agreements, one on rescheduling Damascus' debt to Paris and providing fresh credit to relaunch economic relations, and one on cultural exchanges and training.

Chirac said: "We have put our affairs in order on the economic and financial level." French ministers doggedly refused to say how much of the 1.8 billion franc ($350 million) was being forgiven, how much rescheduled and how much refinanced at lower interest rates to end the decade-old dispute.

French officials belatedly added a visit to the Israeli parliament to Chirac's schedule in the Jewish state after Knesset speaker Dan Tichon, a member of hardline Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party, threatened to boycott him.

It was the second diplomatic row ahead of Chirac's visit following a dispute over French plans to visit a disputed PLO headquarters in Arab East Jerusalem, which Israel says violates interim peace agreements with the Palestinians.
In Damascus, the French leader reiterated his support for a Palestinian state and for the principle of "land for peace", which Netanyahu rejects.
In an apparent effort to avoid offending Assad, he did not repeat past calls for full independence and sovereignty for Lebanon at their joint news conference.

The Syrian leader said they had discussed Lebanon, a former French protectorate, at length in their talks and he defended the presence of some 35,000 Syrian troops there with a long lecture on how his country rescued Lebanon from civil war.
Chirac declined to endorse Syrian assertions that Israel had committed itself to withdrawing from the occupied Golan Heights before talks with Syria broke off earlier this year.

He said that while there had been signed agreements between Israel and the PLO, which must be respected, there had been "deep and positive discussions" between the Jewish state and Syria, which should resume.
